title: Social Media and Teen Mental Health: What the Research Shows
text:
A growing body of research has documented the relationship between social media use and teen mental health. In her 2018 book iGen, psychologist Jean Twenge analyzed generational data from over a million teenagers and found a sharp increase in depression and loneliness beginning around 2012, correlating with the rise of smartphones.

According to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey, 46 percent of teens say social media makes them feel worse about their own lives, while only 9 percent say it makes them feel better.

Not all researchers agree on the magnitude of the effect. A 2022 paper published in Nature Human Behaviour by Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski found that the association between screen time and adolescent well-being is actually quite small — comparable in effect size to wearing glasses. They used a technique called specification curve analysis to test thousands of model specifications and found the effect was not robust.

In 2023, The New York Times published an investigation revealing that Meta's internal research showed Instagram was harmful to teenage girls' body image, based on documents provided by whistleblower Frances Haugen.
